newsitem.title: USA: New catalog gives grandparents leg up on gift giving.
newsitem.headline: New catalog gives grandparents leg up on gift giving.

text.p: If you don't live with children or play with them every day, you may be at a loss when it comes to gift-giving.
Walk down the aisles of a giant toy store and you'll be overwhelmed by the selection. But what toy is appropriate for what child and at what age? For many, this requires some advice.
A new catalogue aimed at grandparents helps them (as well as aunts, uncles, godparents and others) select interesting, safe and age-appropriate toys for the children in their lives.
Gifts for Grandkids, from catalogue retailer Genesis Direct Inc. of Fort Lee, N.J., aims to set itself apart from the mass retailers, offering items that you won't often find at the local mall.

"We took the position that Gifts for Grandkids would be aimed at grandparents. If you don't have small kids yourself, you don't know what is out there; it's not at the top of your mind," said David Sable, one of the principals of Genesis Direct and its chief marketing officer.

About 46 million Americans, or seven out of 10 older adults, have at least one grandchild. Nearly half of all grandparents age 50 and over buy a present for a grandchild in a typical month, according to "Mature America in the 1990s," a report from Modern Maturity magazine and The Roper Organisation.

It is exactly this audience that Sable is hoping to capture. By offering safe toys that are appropriate to a child's age, he said that it makes the task of selecting gifts for a child that much easier.
"We're the front line for the customer. We make choices for them. We cull all the possibilities and make the first cut," Sable said.

It was a Herculean task to winnow down thousands of toys to select 216 for the catalogue, Sable said. Since the catalogue wants to stand apart from mass merchandisers' offerings, there are no licensed, movie tie-in toys or "mass-produced plastic."

The catalogu's offerings are based on classic toys, Sable said, "lasting things for children," including an indoor basketball hoop and a little red wagon. These types of toys foster relationships between the purchaser and the child, he said.
Price was also a consideration in the selection, but Sable said he feels this audience will be willing to pay for better merchandise.
For the youngest children, ages birth to 1 year, the catalogue offers cloth squeeze toys ($20), an activity gym ($35) and a cloth play space with a train motif ($50).
For toddlers up to age 5, there is a tricycle with removable push bar ($120), a spotted dog play mat ($57) and a rocking horse ($110).
As the children age, the toys become more sophisticated. For 5- to 7-year-olds, the catalogue offers a teepee ($137), a race car kit ($100) and wooden U.S. map puzzle ($23).
Toy selections range up to age 12, including a Smithsonian Institute chemistry set ($60), a sports watch ($60) and a loom for making beadwork ($20).
There are also gifts for grandparents, such as shirts, caps, aprons and sweatshirts printed with the grandparent's nickname.

Grandparents are indeed spenders, with the average consumer over age 50 spending $86 on each child at the holidays, according to Research 100, a Princeton, N.J., market research firm. People with annual incomes under $25,000 spend an average of $55, while people with incomes over $75,000 spend an average of $272.
However, many grandparents find it far too difficult to pick out gifts for their grandchildren, so about 60 percent give cash, the Research 100 survey shows.
"That's why we're into this market," said Maria Schupler, Genesis Direct's brand manager. "We see what grandparents spend."
For more information on the Gifts for Grandparents catalogue, call 1-800-333-1707.
